vignette: John, a 49-year-old plumber married to his long-term partner, has been struggling with the aftermath of severe physical abuse inflicted by his romantic partner. The traumatic event occurred in their home when John was trying to resolve an argument that escalated into physical violence. The scent of burnt skin and the memory of his partner's angry outburst have become potent triggers for John's distress. Since the incident, John has come to associate the smell of burning with the intense pain and fear he experienced during the abuse. This olfactory danger cue is particularly disturbing because it often lingers in the air when John is working on plumbing jobs involving hot water heaters or gas lines. The burnt smell can suddenly transport him back to that night, leaving him feeling anxious and trapped. He has started staying up very late to avoid falling asleep with these intrusive thoughts and smells haunting him. John also finds himself avoiding any situations where he might encounter anger from others. His partner's expressions of even calm frustration can send him into a spiral of fear and anxiety. He has begun to delay sleep by distracting himself with work or TV, hoping that the exhaustion will eventually push away his worries and allow him to fall asleep. The memory of the event itself is so distressing that John tries not to think about it at all. This avoidance strategy extends beyond just thoughts; he actively avoids revisiting the site where the abuse took place. His home, which was once a safe haven, now feels like a constant reminder of his trauma. He has started spending more time away from home, often staying late at work or visiting friends to avoid returning. John's efforts to cope by delaying sleep and avoiding reminders have only made things worse. The burnt smell that permeates his workplace is particularly troubling because it acts as an unwelcome reminder every day. Each encounter with anger, whether real or perceived, triggers a flood of anxiety that further disrupts his ability to sleep properly. He often finds himself lying awake, tormented by the thought that another confrontation could lead to another episode of violence. The cumulative effect has taken its toll on John's daily life and relationships. His wife notices the change in him but struggles to understand why he is so distant and irritable. Work colleagues have also observed a decline in his focus and productivity. The combination of avoidance behaviors and maladaptive coping strategies has created a self-reinforcing cycle where each trigger leads to more intense anxiety, further disrupting his sleep and daily functioning. What finally brought John to seek help was the realization that he could no longer ignore how much these symptoms were affecting his life. He is most afraid of another violent outburst from his partner but also hopes for a way to reclaim control over his thoughts and emotions without having to resort to unhealthy coping mechanisms. John wants to find a way to break free from the cycle of fear and avoidance, hoping that with professional support, he can navigate through this ordeal and regain a sense of peace and normalcy in his life.
